s11.slug: FRIDAY · 4:45 AM · THE ANACAPA LOT — THE BLESSING OF TRAVELERS
body: The lamps over the Anacapa lot have burned all night and look it: a tired orange on the asphalt and the bike cage, on the eucalyptus at the far end, on the dew gone gray across every windshield in the rows. It is cold enough to see. Kevin’s mother’s van sits loaded where they left it, hatch down, and the back glass faces the lot the right way round: WHO DAT · 3 DAYS, in white, a day out of date since midnight. Jack hasn’t slept, and his eyes know it.

body.text: Skye wakes up against her window as if somebody had called her name from the next room, sits up, and puts the Saab in gear. She drives the length of the lot with the headlights on, slowly, past the van and the people standing at it, and swings around at the lot’s mouth so the nose points out at Ocean Road, and stops. They get out together, one on each side, and the two doors shut at the same time, two flat sounds. At the van Laney’s head comes around for it, and Theo’s, and Kevin’s. Behind them, through the back windows, three suitcases ride with the belts across them.

Jack is at the hatch in last night’s clothes, his hands in the Carhartt, when the Saab comes in off the road with the top up and the headlights on and noses into the space beside the van. Three suitcases ride in the back seat with the belts across them. Skye gets out in a long black coat with her hair knotted up off her neck and a paper cup in each hand from the 7-Eleven on the loop, comes straight to him, puts one in his hand, and keeps the other.

body: She looks the whole scene over — the van, the orange, the little clouds of breath going up from everybody, the hour on all of them. “Look at this,” she says. “Everybody’s here before call.” She shakes her head at them. “I’d hire every one of you.”

Kevin has the key on one finger and his quarter-zip zipped to the chin. Theo is sitting on the back bumper in a camel coat with his eyes shut, and when Kevin nudges him with a knee he says he is awake, and has been awake, and keeps them shut. Laney is in her Pi Lam sweatshirt with the sleeves pulled down over her hands and sunglasses pushed up on her head at a quarter to five in the morning. Margot is already in her seat, middle left, with the door slid open and her Docs on the running board and Gloria’s box across her knees, both hands on the lid. Past the roof of the van, on the far side, Lena stands by the door to the way-back with her arms folded in a gray hooded sweatshirt. That much comes in at the edge of his eye. He doesn’t look again, and it isn’t hard.
Kevin goes down the van with the key, pointing it at each of them in turn, his lips moving. “Seven,” he says. He stops on Skye. “Six. Sorry. There are seven seats. It gets in your head.”
“Keep one warm,” Skye says.
On the far side of the van Lena speaks, to Kevin. “Kevin. Does he have his license.”
Kevin doesn’t turn around. “Jack. License.”
Jack takes out his wallet and holds it up open over the roof of the van, at the lamps, and puts it back.
“He has his license,” Kevin says.

Father Osei’s small car comes down off Ocean Road with one headlight brighter than the other and parks across two spaces. He gets out in a black anorak and rubber boots to the shin, an aspergillum in one hand and a squeeze bottle of water in the other, and crosses the lot at the pace of the limp, as though five in the morning were a perfectly ordinary hour to be out in a parking lot with equipment.
Kevin puts a hand on the roof of his mother’s van. “Still pretty blessed, Father.”
“It went to Big Sur and came back,” Osei says, unscrewing the head of the aspergillum to fill it from the bottle. “That is all I promise.”
Over the van his eyes find the Saab, the three suitcases belted into it, and then Skye.
“You are traveling too, Skye?”
“Vancouver. Six-forty.”
“Then stand with them.”
She looks at the six of them, and back at him. “What’s my blocking?”
“Stand,” Osei says. “Standing is very ancient.”
“I can do ancient,” Skye says.

So they stand, a ragged circle at the front of the van in the light of the parking lamps Kevin has switched on for it. Theo comes off the bumper. Margot brings the pie. Skye takes the place Osei points her to, between Jack and Theo, and bows her head, and closes her eyes. Jack, beside her, sees it close: her lashes down in the orange, the knot of her hair, her breath going out of her slow and white. Across the hood Lena makes the sign of the cross. Jack makes his.
While Osei talks he puts in one of his own, underneath, short: the six-forty out of Goleta, the whole way up, and down again in two weeks.

“In the book of Tobit,” Osei says, “a young man is sent on a long road, and an angel walks with him the whole way and back, and does not tell him who he is until they are home. May that one go with you.” The aspergillum rests against his boot. “Lord, go before them on the road. Stay with them in the house where they stop. And bring them home to us, all of them — at sixty-five.”
“Amen,” says the circle. Theo’s comes a half second late, and very sincere.

body.text: The water next. Osei goes around with it, a flick of the wrist at a time: the hood, the windshield, the hatch with its white letters, the far side of the van, and then the people, one by one along the circle, Kevin and Margot and the pie and Laney and Theo, and Jack, the same water out of the same bottle as everybody’s. Some of it goes in at his collar and runs down his back, cold.

body: The last of it goes to Skye. She opens her eyes at the touch of it, lifts her hand, and looks at the back of it, at the drops standing on her knuckles in the lamplight, turning it a little, the way she’d hold a contact sheet up to a window.
“Does it work on Saabs?” she asks.

Osei looks across at the Saab and its three suitcases belted in, and goes over to it in his boots, and gives the hood two flicks of the wrist and the windshield one. “It is Swedish,” he says, coming back. “It may need more.”
“It’s GM,” Jack says.
“Don’t,” Skye says, still smiling at her car.
Then she goes down the line.
At the windshield she stops and leans toward the glass, and reads the card taped to the dash beside the chart. “Sixty-five,” she tells Kevin.
“Not sixty-six,” Kevin says, as if it were in the Creed.
“Ted.”
“Callender.”

Theo hugs her longer than a hug usually runs, his chin on her shoulder, and says something into her hair that only she gets. Over her shoulder his face is turned toward the van with its eyes open, and Jack, looking straight at it, can’t read it. Theo lets go of her and is Theo again. “Break a leg. Figuratively. I’ve read the cast insurance.”
“Send me the pilot,” Margot says, over the pie. “I want to see what they do to you.”
“I’ll send you the cut with the notes on it,” Skye says. “You’ll agree with all of them.”
Laney watches her come with the sleeves pulled down over her hands.
“Nice glasses,” Skye says.
Laney brings the sunglasses down off her head onto her nose, in the dark, and looks at her through them. “Knock ’em dead up there.”
Skye goes around the hood to the far side. Jack doesn’t follow her past the headlight; he hears it.
“Have a good trip, Lena. Win your game.”
“Safe flight.”
The sliding door rolls shut on the far side. Through the van’s glass, in the way-back, a gray hood goes up.

Skye comes back around the hood with her hands in her coat pockets, taking her time, the last name on her list. She stops in front of him and looks up at him with the orange on one side of her face. He has been up since yesterday morning, and he is sure of exactly one thing in this lot, and it is standing in front of him with holy water in its hair.
“Read me the margins,” she says. “In that book of yours. Whoever wrote all over it. On the phone, from Texas — not the book, I can buy the book. Them.”
“They’re Hale’s.”
“Then definitely them.”
“Some of them are rude.”
“Those first.”
“Two weeks,” she says. “Then I come back. That’s how this one goes.”

journal.title: Skye Callender
journal.text: Skye Callender, two Ls. Wouldn’t give me a last name — said *Out* — till she texted it to me on the floor in Denver. Met her in a window seat in Montecito, reading O’Connor for a part and had the grandmother exactly backwards. Acts — since she was eleven. Starts here in January: spring, undeclared. She’s declared enough, she says. Doesn’t drink where there are phones. Drives a dented ’91 Saab she says is Swedish. It’s GM. Walked into the Pacific in November like it was a bath, and dared me in after her in my clothes. Asked to kiss me — out loud. She was the one who stopped, in the grandmother’s voice. Typed herself into my phone as SKYE (MISFIT), and called herself from it. Took ten hours to answer my correction. Work, she said — a carpet and a wall. Her car’s an orphan now, and it’s my fault. Nearly three hours at the Starlite, a truck stop up the 101, with Nonna’s pie on the table. Cast me as the Bible salesman. Wanted to know what believing is like — not what I believe. Wants me to miss her a reasonable amount. Get the window, she said. Kissed me again against the Saab in the lot. Slower. On purpose. She was the one who stopped — her thumb on my mouth. She’s on TV. *Sweetwater*, Thursdays at nine: she plays Cassidy, the nice one. Gina screamed. I explained GM to her. In her own car. Thanksgiving: texted me the whole drive from Pittsburgh. Spent it at her mother’s place in Studio City; the parrot says ‘momager.’ Told me not to watch her show. Wants me to be specific. We’re friends on Facebook now — one mutual friend: Theo, who knows everybody. Saturday night she called. Three hours on the porch. Made me do my family. Asked what Advent is. Asked if the TV part matters. Fell asleep in the middle of the Madonna. Monday she drove two hours from LA to sit in a car with me for two more, and set an alarm so she’d leave. Watched the President with the sound off and read his face like a script. Her phone learned a trick in September; she’s still not over it. Gives every truck on the 101 a whole life in three sentences. Knows every word of ‘Thunder Road.’ The tape deck finally let go of *Rumours*. Invited me to LA; I work Saturdays. Doesn’t take people home. Saturday, in daylight, on a rock above the tide pools: fractions, for the placement test. I drew her a pie. Sharks were a lie. I told her a saint broke in. Drove me to Burbank in the rain to be her cousin from Ohio. Everybody on a set wants something from her; she smiles for every phone. Plays a preacher’s daughter who forgives a thief. She played it dry. Washed a borrowed dress in a laundromat at one in the morning; it lived. Thinks the Immaculate Conception is the other one. Took the math test with forty kids and nobody looked at her once. Doesn’t take people home. Took me home. Lives on Del Playa, in a house with a darkroom she isn’t allowed in and two boards under the porch the boys won’t let on the rack — she’ll live there in January. On her bed I said no. She stopped everything and asked me why, and we talked till it got light. I told her it’s a no right now. She said she can work with that. Picked my present for the church party: a Magic 8-Ball. Every answer’s a line reading, she says. Her car died in Buellton; I pushed. She’s seen Our Lady of Guadalupe on every taco truck in the Valley and thought she was a brand. Friday night she took my ‘right now’ apart, point by point, with visual aids, and made a very good case. It’s still right now. I said no again, and she stopped right there and nowhere else. Came to the Anchor in my shirt; Gloria rated her boysenberry. She’s going to ask every day, she says. It’s in her calendar. Slept at her house. Just slept. She says that doesn’t happen. Taught me to surf at Ellery on Gaudete Sunday. I’m terrible. I go home in six days. She isn’t counting. Played Hale in her car from my description. Made me answer the question I couldn’t at the Starlite. Thursday at one in the morning, no moon at all, she drove the bluff with the lights off. Not before Christmas, she said — Christmas and New Year’s and long distance are too much for something new. When I get back we’re dating. Officially. A whole thing. She counted. GM is killing Saab. I’m on the hook. Christmas week: Theo’s known her since they were eleven — his father’s company makes her show. She calls him Ted; nobody else does. She saw us walk into the Hallorans’ together and hid behind a ficus. “Peace mission” was for him. He ran into her at a party in the hills on the twenty-second, and she says he knows. She had me do the weather barefoot in the snow. Seventeen days; she’s not counting. Christmas morning my family found her — Gina gave me her show on DVD. They know her as the nice one. She wants it on her headstone. The day after Christmas my whole family watched season two of her show. She was eighteen, in a blazer, on a dock. She’s good — Dad said so, and she says nobody says good. Nonna prays for Cassidy now. She bought Chesterton used on Ventura without knowing it was my book, and wants to know who picked midnight. The Monday after Christmas she called, and we talked till my phone died. New Year’s Eve she watched my ball drop on the East Coast feed at nine her time and texted, so she’d be at midnight with me. Then she had her own, at three in the morning mine, from a locked den in the hills. I told her I called Ted *Ted*. She says he’s right: that one’s hers. She has my flight home written on her hand. She read Matthew 2 because I said Sunday was Epiphany; Herod is a jealous showrunner. OFFICIALLY, in eyeliner, on a sign at the rope at Santa Barbara, in sunglasses at night. A girl from my flight filmed it, and by morning it was on a gossip blog. Skye put the still on her own Facebook herself. Her people wanted lunch: her mother, Debbie, who manages her, and her publicist, Corinne. The rules: no pictures, ‘a friend from school,’ February. Take the airport down. She took it down. There was a folder with my last name on it, and she pushed it back without opening it. At a gas station in Buellton she took the first picture of the two of us herself, at arm’s length, and put it up instead. Then she changed her status herself and made me say yes to it on her phone — the first thing anybody ever watched her do that nobody wrote. Monday she came to the Fishbowl and argued with me about a rose. My pie got her out of remedial math. Tuesday she taught me stick in an empty lot — a voice for every stall. I do a bad Frank. We argued Conan. She posted a picture of me stalling. The radio, at 2:31: Haiti. At midnight she took the picture down — not for Corinne. Wednesday in the Brick she explained the plates under Haiti from her Oceanography book, read me Milton off the front of *Frankenstein*, and fell asleep on my shoulder. At the Haiti table she borrowed Becca’s apron and was Cassidy for twenty dollars a name, and asked me where God was at 4:53. Met Laney. Met everybody. Corinne wanted a statement; she told her the girl at the table was right about the pictures, and hung up. That night she asked me to say one for them, from her. ‘Saturday.’ Thursday Margot interviewed her at the Anchor; she says I’m the same in every room. Saturday at dawn she taught me again, inside the Point. Still very bad at it. She posted it and kept it up. She came to Sully’s and learned the Who Dat. Laney took a shot at her; she had it handled, she says, and I didn’t let her finish, and she says she’ll reward that sort of behavior. In the Saab I told her some about Lena — that we were close in the fall. She said she can tell there’s a rest. She drove me to confession, and went back to Sully’s without me. Saturday night she read me Sunday’s Gospel off her phone. Three nights in LA: a fitting for the wedding episode — she’s not the bride, she checked. Tuesday she made me explain Massachusetts while I walked. The tornado took Sol’s swing. Wednesday she drove home with the top down in the rain and put the two of us up on Facebook, soaked. Thursday we argued the Supreme Court under one umbrella until it turned inside out. She’s been a corporation since she was twelve — Skylark Pictures; her mother named it. She wrote my brother, in capitals; Rudy says write the number big. Friday the sun came out, and she called the telethon as Skylark. Saturday she drove six hours to the Walk for Life, walked the whole thing arguing with me, and stood in front of Clare when a man started screaming. Sunday she came to Mass. I told her why I didn’t go up. Out past the break I told her what I know about the basement, which isn’t much, and about Nonna’s question and Danny’s. She’s the answer to both. She knows there’s more; she said that’s enough. She asked me to teach her Nonna’s prayer. Monday a blog found the back of my head; Gina knew Danny’s jacket before the commenters did. Corinne called her at six: every picture of us down until there’s a strategy. At noon in her room I was the one who didn’t want to stop, and she stopped it — for Sunday. She’d read up on confession to do it: I can’t walk in on Wednesday with a plan, and she won’t be my plan. Ask her again after she’s watched me go up. She asked me what I lose when I sit in the pew, and I told her: they pass the plate over you. She watched them do it on Sunday and didn’t know what she was watching. Then she took a picture of us without looking, and that night she put it up, captioned with Corinne’s own rule — *my friend from school.* At the lunch in Studio City her shoes stayed on. When they got to Danny she came back for that and nothing else, and said his number from memory. In the car she said she’s very good at fine. She heard me tell Ma *tomorrow*, and that I think she’s the answer, and took the picture down at the Las Posas exit without a word. Sol’s swing is up. I told her I don’t care, and she could tell. She’s stopping anyway. She wants Nonna to like her. Wednesday she said Theo and Laney were running lines. Wednesday night she was at the curb when I got home from confession. She asked if I went. Then, in the middle of a bit about a Supreme Court justice, I said it first. I didn’t know I was going to. She’d been carrying it since Monday, and she was going to say it first. She said it back. Thursday she took me to a fundraiser in the Palisades and never said what for — it didn’t occur to her anybody would mind. It was for Boxer: Corinne wanted me in the picture so the march would stop being a story. She saw my face across the room and asked twice. I told her it was fine — she came to my Walk and took the other side seriously, so I could stand in hers. So she went back in and got the whole room to argue with me, the real arguments, in Gil’s living room, for two hours, and made sure every one of them knew where I stand. We stayed till the end. At a taquería at the bottom of Sunset she wouldn’t post Corinne’s picture. She blew me a raspberry and posted one of us at the table instead: we agree on each other, and we’re not just friends from school. She’s a union member. Two of them. Her father was Pat Doyle, a juicer on the Meridian lots, gone since she was four. Then she said her name. Mary Catherine Callender-Doyle. Baptized at St. Mary’s in Lancaster, named for his mother. The only name she has that her mother didn’t give her. I sent the first two to Gina for Nonna. At three in the morning I made the picture my profile picture. She says I stole her art. She says happy looks good on me. Friday she argued Margot to a draw and went home to learn lines. Saturday at the Point I told her Nonna lit a candle for Maria Caterina. Saturday night on the bluff she kept her word: tomorrow. Sunday she sat in the same pew, in a cardigan she bought for Mass, and watched me go up, and knelt. That night she asked first, before anything. I told her it’s still no, for now. And that it’s closer than it’s ever been. She asked what question she’s the answer to. I told her Nonna asked me what makes me pray. She asked if she does. Yes. She wants to be the good thing, with the lights off. I stayed. Just sleep. Monday she picked Danny’s birthday book on State Street — O’Connor, all the stories — and wrote the card herself, in capitals. She says Gretta’s the only one at that party who isn’t acting. At a red light the radio played it, the day before his birthday, and we sang it at each other with the top down. Somebody filmed it. Tuesday her people were on the phone by six. She didn’t share it; she wrote on my wall instead: bring the clean version next time. I told her I was sorry about her job. She kissed me on the Morro steps in front of everybody and told me never to apologize for making her happy. Then Danny called on his birthday and she got on the phone. She told him I tricked her. Then she told him the truth: she was about to leave when I walked over, and she still has the book, with CON crossed out. Candlemas she held my candle while I knelt. That night she came up to my room for the first time. She didn’t ask. When she asks again, she says, she wants me to have nowhere to be in the morning. She asked if there’s a version of later she’s in. Wednesday on the swing, coats on, she kept me in the daylight. She’s in Vancouver for two weeks, a pilot, from Friday. She told me to go to New Orleans and watch my Saints win. Maybe it’ll be good for you guys, she said. I said yes. Thursday we skipped the rest of the day for the Point. Sol let her into the darkroom in January, for the project. Thursday night it was full of me — asleep, the back of me on the Point, the two of us on the swing — pictures I didn’t know anybody was taking. She gave me the swing: NOT FOR POSTING. It’s in Hale’s book. She propped the door open on purpose. She asked, and I said yes, and she was the one who said no. Her father called her Mary Kate. He left in the dark for a five o’clock call when she was four, kissed her, told her to go back to sleep, and didn’t come back. Everybody she’s ever loved had a call time. When I come back she wants the truth, to her face. I promised. She drove me up the hill at three and waited in the Saab under the bell tower with three suitcases in the back. Friday at a quarter to five she stood with us in the lot while Osei blessed the van, with her eyes shut, and looked at the water on the back of her hand. Bye, Coat check. She went north. We went south.

Saturday at dawn she taught me again, inside the Point. Still very bad at it. She posted it and kept it up. She came to Sully’s and learned the Who Dat. Laney took a shot at her; she had it handled, she says, and I didn’t let her finish, and she says she’ll reward that sort of behavior. In the Saab I told her some about Lena — that we were close in the fall. She said she can tell there’s a rest. She drove me to confession, and went back to Sully’s without me. Saturday night she read me Sunday’s Gospel off her phone. Three nights in LA: a fitting for the wedding episode — she’s not the bride, she checked. Tuesday she made me explain Massachusetts while I walked. The tornado took Sol’s swing. Wednesday she drove home with the top down in the rain and put the two of us up on Facebook, soaked. Thursday we argued the Supreme Court under one umbrella until it turned inside out. She’s been a corporation since she was twelve — Skylark Pictures; her mother named it. She wrote my brother, in capitals; Rudy says write the number big. Friday the sun came out, and she called the telethon as Skylark. Saturday she drove six hours to the Walk for Life, walked the whole thing arguing with me, and stood in front of Clare when a man started screaming. Sunday she came to Mass. I told her why I didn’t go up. Out past the break I told her what I know about the basement, which isn’t much, and about Nonna’s question and Danny’s. She’s the answer to both. She knows there’s more; she said that’s enough. She asked me to teach her Nonna’s prayer. Monday a blog found the back of my head; Gina knew Danny’s jacket before the commenters did. Corinne called her at six: every picture of us down until there’s a strategy. At noon in her room I was the one who didn’t want to stop, and she stopped it — for Sunday. She’d read up on confession to do it: I can’t walk in on Wednesday with a plan, and she won’t be my plan. Ask her again after she’s watched me go up. She asked me what I lose when I sit in the pew, and I told her: they pass the plate over you. She watched them do it on Sunday and didn’t know what she was watching. Then she took a picture of us without looking, and that night she put it up, captioned with Corinne’s own rule — *my friend from school.* At the lunch in Studio City her shoes stayed on. When they got to Danny she came back for that and nothing else, and said his number from memory. In the car she said she’s very good at fine. She heard me tell Ma *tomorrow*, and that I think she’s the answer, and took the picture down at the Las Posas exit without a word. Sol’s swing is up. I told her I don’t care, and she could tell. She’s stopping anyway. She wants Nonna to like her. Wednesday she said Theo and Laney were running lines. Wednesday night she was at the curb when I got home from confession. She asked if I went. Then, in the middle of a bit about a Supreme Court justice, I said it first. I didn’t know I was going to. She’d been carrying it since Monday, and she was going to say it first. She said it back. Thursday she took me to a fundraiser in the Palisades and never said what for — it didn’t occur to her anybody would mind. It was for Boxer: Corinne wanted me in the picture so the march would stop being a story. She saw my face across the room and asked twice. I told her it was fine — she came to my Walk and took the other side seriously, so I could stand in hers. So she went back in and got the whole room to argue with me, the real arguments, in Gil’s living room, for two hours, and made sure every one of them knew where I stand. We stayed till the end. At a taquería at the bottom of Sunset she wouldn’t post Corinne’s picture. She blew me a raspberry and posted one of us at the table instead: we agree on each other, and we’re not just friends from school. She’s a union member. Two of them. Her father was Pat Doyle, a juicer on the Meridian lots, gone since she was four. Then she said her name. Mary Catherine Callender-Doyle. Baptized at St. Mary’s in Lancaster, named for his mother. The only name she has that her mother didn’t give her. I sent the first two to Gina for Nonna. At three in the morning I made the picture my profile picture. She says I stole her art. She says happy looks good on me. Friday she argued Margot to a draw and went home to learn lines. Saturday at the Point I told her Nonna lit a candle for Maria Caterina. Saturday night on the bluff she kept her word: tomorrow. Sunday she sat in the same pew, in a cardigan she bought for Mass, and watched me go up, and knelt. That night she asked first, before anything. I told her it’s still no, for now. And that it’s closer than it’s ever been. She asked what question she’s the answer to. I told her Nonna asked me what makes me pray. She asked if she does. Yes. She wants to be the good thing, with the lights off. I stayed. Just sleep. Monday she picked Danny’s birthday book on State Street — O’Connor, all the stories — and wrote the card herself, in capitals. She says Gretta’s the only one at that party who isn’t acting. At a red light the radio played it, the day before his birthday, and we sang it at each other with the top down. Somebody filmed it. Tuesday her people were on the phone by six. She didn’t share it; she wrote on my wall instead: bring the clean version next time. I told her I was sorry about her job. She kissed me on the Morro steps in front of everybody and told me never to apologize for making her happy. Then Danny called on his birthday and she got on the phone. She told him I tricked her. Then she told him the truth: she was about to leave when I walked over, and she still has the book, with CON crossed out. Candlemas she held my candle while I knelt. That night she came up to my room for the first time. She didn’t ask. When she asks again, she says, she wants me to have nowhere to be in the morning. She asked if there’s a version of later she’s in. Wednesday on the swing, coats on, she kept me in the daylight. She’s in Vancouver for two weeks, a pilot, from Friday. She told me to go to New Orleans and watch my Saints win. Maybe it’ll be good for you guys, she said. I said yes. Thursday we skipped the rest of the day for the Point. Sol let her into the darkroom in January, for the project. Thursday night it was full of me — asleep, the back of me on the Point, the two of us on the swing — pictures I didn’t know anybody was taking. She gave me the swing: NOT FOR POSTING. It’s in Hale’s book. She propped the door open on purpose. She asked, and I said yes, and she was the one who said no. Her father called her Mary Kate. He left in the dark for a five o’clock call when she was four, kissed her, told her to go back to sleep, and didn’t come back. Everybody she’s ever loved had a call time. When I come back she wants the truth, to her face. I promised. I walked up the hill alone at three. Friday at a quarter to five she came to the lot with three suitcases and stood with us while Osei blessed the van, with her eyes shut, and looked at the water on the back of her hand. Bye, Coat check. She went north. We went south.

journal.title: Kevin Tran
journal.text: Kevin Tran. Goes to daily Mass, saves you a seat with a Bible. Has a sister, Tina, in dental school, who flossed in the womb. Lies to his mom about orgo in Vietnamese. Drives his mother’s Odyssey at sixty-five, not sixty-six. His dad has two nail-salon supply stores in San Jose and has never had a Labor Day. Brought six pairs of gloves to a beach cleanup. Mouthed every word of Joey’s first reading from the second pew. Somebody coached Joey; I can guess who. Brought tea to a wake. His Bà Nội says heaven makes the elephant and heaven makes the grass. Walked Margot down at four in the morning. Handed Lena a roll of quarters for the payphone before she asked. Halloween: All Saints, every one nobody’s heard of — scrubs, a halo and a white mask. He found Laney. Friday night a pre-med said Maine got it right. Kevin answered him and went to get water. Tuesday, the Vietnamese Martyrs: his mother reads eleven of the hundred and seventeen. Asked about the scar. Alarm Five, on the lawn: he had a question mark next to my name on his clipboard. I told Priya I was out. He erased it. Tuesday at four I woke him for Doug. A chair under the knob, then a bell. Wednesday at the Brick, at the next carrel all night: ‘You two have been defending each other for three hours. That isn’t studying.’ Sings bass. A real one. Seven years of Vietnamese choir in San Jose — his mother made him. Friday, from the Odyssey: Go home. Sleep. Tell somebody something. Back from San Jose. His mother has a girl from their parish she wants him to call. Clare. She plays the violin in the Mass band. Wednesday he brought two flats of water to the Haiti table, which nobody asked for, and stayed to hold Clare’s violin case. ‘My mother knows your mother.’ Thursday he called Clare. His mother had the number, and his grandmother was on the speaker. She said yes to Sully’s. MLK Day he brought gloves for everybody. Tuesday in the basement he read us the first reading off his BlackBerry. Clare’s going to the Walk for Life, and so is he. He asked me to come — for him. I said yes. Thursday at the window table he had a list: things to say at hour four. He’d heard about Hale’s — Laney to Margot to him — and didn’t take a side. Then he asked me what you’re supposed to feel at hour four. I told him. He wrote it down. Clare asked him which of us was right at Hale’s; he told her he didn’t have the information, and she said that was a very Kevin answer. He asked if my brother’s okay. Thursday night at the van he had a clipboard and a seating chart taped to the dash, and said he’s pre-med, not a switchboard. Clare came to see him off. At three in the morning he was at St. Brendan’s ahead of me. Couldn’t sleep either. At a quarter to five Osei blessed his mother’s car again. Still pretty blessed.

choices.text: *Kiss her like nobody’s in the lot.*
choices.key: At a quarter to five in the Anacapa lot you kissed Skye goodbye like nobody was watching.
response: He kisses her like there’s nobody in the lot. It’s meant to be the short one, the one you give somebody at a curb, and it doesn’t stay short. Her mouth is warm and her nose is cold against his cheek; her hand comes up and takes hold of his collar where the holy water went in, and keeps the wet corduroy in her fist, and he has his arms inside her coat, around the warm of her back through a sweater. It goes past where a goodbye at a curb stops, and past where the next one would, until she laughs against his mouth and has to come up for air. Her rings are cold on the back of his neck. From very close her eyes go over his face, eyebrow to jaw, like somebody checking a frame before she prints it.

She kisses him once more, short, the real short one, with her fist still in his collar. “Bye, Coat check.” She lets go of the corduroy and smooths it down where she had it, and walks to the Saab, and gets in.

She reaches for the deck before she touches anything else. The tape in it starts at the beginning of a song: a piano, and one woman’s voice. She runs the window down to let it out, and the Saab pulls away with the piano coming up out of the open window into the dark, and at the mouth of the lot she taps the horn twice, short, and turns north toward the airport, and the eucalyptus takes the sound.

Kevin says, “Okay,” to the asphalt, and the van’s doors slide and slam one after another, and Jack is in his seat, middle right, with the water still down his back. As the Odyssey starts to roll, Father Osei steps up beside it and lays his palm on its flank, just under Jack’s window, and walks a few steps with it like that, and lets it go. In Theo’s side mirror he is standing in the emptied lot with the aspergillum at his side when Kevin makes the turn.

choices.text: “A doubloon and the worst T-shirt in Louisiana.”
choices.key: At a quarter to five in the Anacapa lot you promised Skye a doubloon and the worst T-shirt in Louisiana.
response: “A doubloon,” he says. “And the worst T-shirt in Louisiana.”

“Caught,” Skye says. She takes both his hands out of the Carhartt and holds them up between their two faces in the lamplight, palms out. “With your own two hands. These ones. I’ll know.” She turns them over and looks at the backs, where Osei’s water has dried, and kisses the knuckles of the left one, and gives them back to him.
“I’ll catch it in my teeth if I have to.”
“You’ll catch it with your hands, like a Christian,” she says.
“Where’s that, Leviticus?”
“Second Hezekiah. Look it up.”

Her keys are already out, the Saab’s fob hanging off one finger. She comes up on her toes and kisses him, quick, and the fob knocks cold against his jaw. “Bye, Coat check.” And she is walking, and then she is in the Saab.

At the mouth of the lot the brake lights come on. Her arm goes across to the glovebox, and she feeds a cassette into the deck and runs the window down, and a piano comes out of the Saab into the dark lot, and one woman’s voice over it. Two short taps on the horn. She turns north for the airport, and the music goes up the road with her until he can’t sort it from the wind in the eucalyptus.

Behind Jack the doors are already sliding shut, one after another, Laney’s last and hardest. He gets in, middle right. Kevin lets the brake off, and as the van starts to move Father Osei puts his hand out and rests his palm on its flank beside Jack’s window, walking with it a few steps, until it pulls away from under his hand. Jack watches him in Theo’s side mirror, a man in rubber boots holding an aspergillum in an empty parking lot, still standing there when the turn takes him.

choices.key: At a quarter to five in the Anacapa lot you told Skye you’d call her at the kickoff.
response: “I’ll call you at the kickoff,” he says.

She looks at him. Something in her face settles, as if a scene she’s been playing has turned out to have a floor under it. “I’ll be in a trailer,” she says. “In a wig, probably, with a man named Gord doing my eyebrows. Call anyway.”
“I’ll call anyway.”
“Let it ring. They’ll come and get me.”
“And if they lose?”
“Then you call me first.” She takes his face in both cold hands and kisses him, and lets go. “Bye, Coat check.”

She walks to the Saab without looking back and gets in. The window comes down first, all the way, before anything else, and lets the cold into the car; then the tape, and a piano out of it, and one woman’s voice, coming across the lot to the van. The Saab pulls away. At the mouth of the lot she gives the horn two short taps and turns north toward the airport, and he listens to the piano go up the road until it’s gone into the trees.

The van’s doors slide and slam, and Kevin has the engine going before Jack has his seat belt across him. As they roll, Father Osei walks beside the Odyssey a few steps with his palm on its flank under Jack’s window, the way you’d walk a horse out of a barn, and then the van is going faster than a man with a limp, and his hand comes away. Theo’s side mirror keeps him: the anorak, the boots, the aspergillum, standing under the lamps until Kevin makes the turn.

s12.slug: FRIDAY · 6:48 AM · US-101 SOUTH, THE RINCON — TAG
body: At the Rincon the first gray comes up behind the mountains on the left and lies out across the water on the right, and the platforms offshore are still dark, a light or two on each. Kevin has the Odyssey at sixty-five exactly, both hands on the wheel, the La Vang rosary swinging under the mirror and Clare’s holy card in the visor over his head. Off Rincon Point two surfers are already sitting on their boards in the gray, waiting on a set, and Jack watches them until the road bends them out of his window.

body.text: Theo is asleep in the passenger seat in MEDIUM SPARKLE’s satin sleep mask, his head against the window and his mouth open, like a silent-film heiress somebody has poisoned at a house party.
body.else: Theo is asleep in the passenger seat with his own hand over his eyes, his head against the window, as though the dawn had said something he didn’t care for.

body.text: Across the aisle Margot is awake with the boysenberry on her knees, Gloria’s rating ringed in grease pencil on the lid and one corner of the box gone purple overnight. She has both hands on it.
body.else: Across the aisle Margot is awake with the pecan on her knees, Gloria’s rating ringed in grease pencil on the lid, facing up. She has both hands on it.

body: Behind him Laney is asleep against the way-back window with her sunglasses still on.
Margot sees him look at the box. “It’s structurally sound,” she says, low, not turning her head. “I’ve been checking since Montecito.”
The song changes on Kevin’s mix, two guitars and a lot of road in them. Theo speaks from wherever he is, without moving. “Kevin.”
“It’s the *right road*,” Kevin says.
Theo accepts this and goes back under.
After the dead stretch by Carpinteria the RAZR finds its bar and buzzes twice against his leg.

body.text: at the gate. window seat. im going north and youre going south and im fine about it

body: The second one came a minute after the first. He likes the minute best.

Up front Kevin catches his eye in the mirror and lifts a hand off the wheel, and puts it back. Jack keeps the phone low on his knee, where the light from it doesn’t reach anybody, and types with his thumb.

body.text: mostly fine here too. kevins doing 65
He shuts the phone, and somewhere ahead of him in a city he has never seen there is a doubloon he hasn’t caught yet, already in his head, in the shape of a promise.

body: By now the six-forty is off the ground in Goleta, or about to be, and turning north over the water.

body.text: Back by Summerland he said what he has of Mark 6 again, against the glass, under the mix, nobody’s penance: no bread, no bag, no money in the belt, a walking stick. He has a duffel, a borrowed book, a photograph and sixty-one dollars’ worth of a seat, and no stick at all.
body.else: Back by Summerland he said his penance over again against the glass, under the mix, to be sure of the morning: no bread, no bag, no money in the belt, a walking stick. He has a duffel, a borrowed book, a photograph and sixty-one dollars’ worth of a seat, and no stick at all.

body: Hale’s *Moviegoer* is open on his knee to where the print is. It lies between the pages with its back up, her capitals across it in grease pencil — NOT FOR POSTING — and the last letters smeared where her wrist went through them. On the left-hand page Hale has underlined a few words about a search, years ago, in his small upright hand, and written beside them: *He calls it a search. It is a stakeout.*
Behind him and to the left, in the way-back, Lena rides with her hood up and her face to her window. That is where Kevin’s chart put her, so that Jack wouldn’t have to see her, and he doesn’t.
The van goes south under the gray at sixty-five, and Jack rides with the book open on his knee and his thumb on the edge of the print, on the corner that curls.

journal.title: Theo Vance
journal.text: Roommate. Drives his grandfather’s car like a getaway. His father calls him Teddy and stays six minutes. Heard my brother’s voice and didn’t ask. Loves *Point Break* with no irony at all. Poppy texts him at midnight. The Big Sur Expedition, on his father’s letterhead. Called the Anchor and got my Saturday covered before I could say I work Saturdays. Bought six used copies of Kerouac off the cart at Driftwood. Halloween: threw the party of the year as Gatsby. Left it at twelve-thirty by the back gate. Found him at the wall at the Point at one in the morning, the second one. He said not there. Nineteen. His father sent a stretch Lincoln and a card that called him Teddy, and called at six minutes past and stayed four. His mother came up from La Cañada with Poppy. Blew out nineteen candles in one breath. Sunday night, to the ceiling: Laney says he asked if he could ask. ‘Like a vampire. They have to be invited in.’ He’s known since Friday. Wednesday I said I ended it. He opened his jar and gave me a spoon. Friday he took me to a party in Montecito so I wouldn’t meet anybody, and lost me in three minutes. Saturday at six he was on his bed in his coat. He’d called me nine times. At halftime of Michigan I asked him home for Thanksgiving. He said yes before I finished, and bought two tickets to Pittsburgh. ‘Guests bring something.’ Looked up St. Elizabeth’s visiting hours before I asked. Thanksgiving: came to Youngstown in Dad’s Browns parka over the camel coat. Dad said that’s not a coat. Speaks Italian from a movie, wrong. Rolled Nonna’s crust and made his own peach pie. Dad asked him to say grace. He did. Nonna asked who prays for him; he said nobody. Met Danny — Danny liked him in a minute. Didn’t talk the whole way home. Kept Rosie’s prince. Nonna gave him a twenty. Back at Marisol he reads me the News Feed in the morning like the intentions at the twelve-ten. Wants to know if I *like* things now. Says I’m fast. Says I’ve started sleeping with my phone. Played the Fishbowl a voicemail off the internet and ran one sentence of it twice: take your name off your phone. Timed my pocket with his stopwatch. Didn’t say the number. Taped Rosie’s princes over his desk; Nonna’s twenty is in the frame of his mirror. Covered for me at Alarm Five: I was in the shower. Sat on a dryer with Laney, discussing finals. Sunday at twenty to seven: back from somewhere. I asked him home for Christmas; so did Pop, in the garage. He has things in LA. ‘Tell your father I heard him.’ Put his cashmere on me Sunday. Said I was holding my phone like a rosary. Lent me the Burberry in the storm. Tried to heckle Julian’s song and couldn’t. Watched me go through Bastille’s window. Six in the morning on the last day of classes he asked why I look like I’ve been through a war. He had a question in his calendar for after Thanksgiving; he’s moved it. Sunday he filmed his shoes with a girl named Soledad. Tore up the tab. Left me his cashmere for Ohio. Have a good Christmas, Costigan — all of it. Christmas: called from LA to ask for Christmas Eve and Christmas Day. I answered on the first ring; he sounded surprised. Dad said he doesn’t have to call first. Wore the parka again. Ma glued his name on a stocking. Nonna has his cashmere. Ate an eel. Took my phone out of Rosie’s hand at dinner and gave it to me face-down. Christmas Eve he came with me to Trumbull, bought from the machines, and did Dad for Danny. Danny asked him who comes to see him. He said I do. Danny says he’s on the list for good. Wears the Browns hat now. Laney has a schedule. Landed in the middle of the night — they wanded the baccalà in Pittsburgh. At the side door Christmas afternoon he said, Be careful, Costigan. Of what. All of it. New Year’s Eve, at nine his time, the party was already a disappointment. Wore Ma’s scarf in sixty-one degrees. A woman asked if he was in a band. Back from LA in the orange hat and Ma’s scarf. Says the hat is a family heirloom. Sunday night: ‘Congratulations, Costigan.’ ‘Go to sleep. Monday is going to be a long day.’ Tuesday morning he did the responses too: Lord, hear our prayer. Rushing Sigma Rho; ate a raw onion in front of the lacrosse team. Wednesday night he got a bid. A pledge now. Carries a raw egg named Hollis in a teacup; if it breaks, he’s out. At Sully’s: ‘She’s the best actress I know, Costigan. Never ask her if she’s acting.’ MLK Day he shoveled sand one-handed for Sigma Rho with Hollis in the other. At midnight Wednesday he pitched me a movie about a man whose friend got dumped and was with somebody else in a week. He said it twice. Hollis made his week. Theo’s in. He’s keeping the egg. Saturday he became a brother. Sunday he runs. He was correct to Lena for seven hours at Sully’s and sent me the end of it. He started on Julian, and I told him to stop. Monday he asked me, hypothetically, where a man who doesn’t go to Sully’s watches the Super Bowl. Made himself my plus-one to Hale’s, with a bottle that had a story. Tuesday morning I told him I think she’s the answer. He wanted a pamphlet, framed. Then he said nobody ever asked her to be that, and an answer is heavy for the person you hand it to. At Hale’s door Laney told him that wasn’t about a book. He said no. At midnight, to the ceiling: don’t ever make me watch that again. Thursday he dressed me for the Palisades: his charcoal suit, pinned, and a half-Windsor — a commitment, like a coat. In the mirror he said I was good at it Wednesday, and that’s what he didn’t like. Friday: “You stayed.” She kept me there. “That’s love.” Saturday I tied his for the Pi Lam formal. He wanted the January call word for word. I gave it to him once. He asked if I know what I’m going to say tomorrow, if she asks. Monday: six days. Hollis was concerned; he told him I’d been detained by the Holy See. Monday night, two legal pads with Laney: a wedding seating chart, hypothetical. Tuesday he said Sigma Rho till two and left me the room. At a quarter to two he was in the lounge with Laney, Margot and Kevin: book club, *Dubliners*. He came in at twenty past two. Wednesday he pitched me New Orleans like a movie — the Saints, the money, and then, for the first time since I’ve known him, a favor. I need you there. I said no. That night I said yes, by text, from the stairs. Kevin drives the first shift. I drive West Texas. Thursday night he’d already paid my share. I made him take it back. He took a call from his mother at the edge of the lot: sandbags; they’re saying rain Friday night on the hill. At a quarter to five he hugged Skye a long time and said something only she heard.

journal.title: Lena Broussard
journal.text: New Orleans. Two seventeen. Classics. Hale paired us for the semester. Makes a roux like she’s taking a vow and expects you to keep up. Her father sells Gulf shrimp — Broussard’s Seafood, Banks Street. Boyfriend: Wes Arceneaux — Tulane, civil engineering, the boat at sixteen. Calls at 8:04 on the dot. Her grandmother, Lucille Guidry, died in the storm in ’05; they buried her in November, in the good dress. The medal came back to her mother in a plastic bag. She has never asked her mother one question. The year after, she went to Mass every morning to yell at God, and somewhere in there it stopped being a fight. Paints a mean fleur-de-lis. Said hi to Danny. Says she’s going to be defense. Walked her home the long way from Pi Lam: the beach, the creek, the tower, the Commons, the Lagoon bench. Wes calls from somewhere loud lately; her brother Luc is with him. She’s decided not to notice. The Tuesday of the wake he called on the dot, from his room. He came for Columbus Day weekend to see the Pacific. She’d told him it’s a threat. He touched it at two in the morning. Came to Marisol for the money, she says — Notre Dame gave her half. Went to Hale’s office to tell him he was wrong about who gets to forgive. Cried for Anders on the roof and didn’t give an inch. Stayed till the chimes. There’s a sentence she hasn’t finished. Her middle name is Thérèse; October first is her feast. She erased *Show Lena* out of the Hopkins herself, so Danny could have it. At midnight I gave her *Story of a Soul* with my margins in it, and she wouldn’t let me erase a word. On the beach she asked if I know what I’m doing. I don’t. She laughed. At the elevator: ‘That was a terrible thing to be glad about.’ Brought Wes to everything. Wouldn’t walk past the last house on Seacliff toward the Point; said she was cold. At the stove she gave Becca the spoon. Monday night, two floors down, on the phone to New Orleans: ‘He’s my friend, Wes.’ Plays the piano in the Delgado basement — the one nobody admits to playing. Two years at the Rosary. At five in the morning she played the Saints on the Ferrer carillon with her fists, one bell flat, and said it wasn’t flat, it was New Orleans. Wes told her what I said on the beach, and what I didn’t. On a motel porch above Lucia at three in the morning she told me I can’t say her name like that. She asked what I decided. Not to be the one who wrecks anything, I said. She said okay. Then: me neither. Bought her Mémère a fruitcake from the monks, in exact change. ‘A girl writes the thing she wants first, Youngstown.’ Halloween: Flannery O’Connor, with a stuffed peacock tagged 57. Andalusia. She wouldn’t go past the last house on Seacliff, not even for Laney. ‘I came as her. I never said she was right.’ In the last minute of the extra hour, she put my hat back on. All Souls: she wrote her grandmother’s name in the book, and Nora Calloway’s. Nora was her host at Preview Weekend, in April. That night Wes ended it, on the phone, on the east stairs. He stopped going to Mass in September. There’s a ring. She knew something in September and decided not to notice — she says she’s good at it. At six in the morning she asked me what I’m going to do. She wrote Hale twelve pages in the spring of ’08, two years after the year she yelled at God. She’s had the same postcard the whole time. She knew mine on the porch. She had a house picked out on Zimple Street. A fig tree. She’d picked the paint. Veterans Day, on the bench above Campus Point: St. Martin gave the beggar half his cloak; she says everybody forgets the beggar took it. No. 9 for the reliquary. Friday the 13th, under the eucalyptus, in the middle of a sentence about monarchs: Julian asked her to dinner. So. Thursday night in the basement she played the piano properly — around the dead F. The last time she played it right in front of anybody was a November, four years ago. If you play well, she says, people ask you to play. Reading *New Moon* out of spite. Friday she signed the Manhattan Declaration from bed, with a cold. Two soups. She ate Julian’s. Mine’s on the sill for tomorrow. Ate Gloria’s soup cold out of the quart, at the sill, at six in the morning. Argued YES: a promise is made to a person, not to a reason. Wrote on my paper that I don’t believe one sentence of it. Neither does she. Mémère is lighting a candle for Nonna — the whole name. Half a name is half a candle. At the airport: Our Lady of Prompt Succor, for Nonna. She works fast. Thanksgiving: Theo said *pop* to the whole Broussard table. She asked about Theo, and Nonna, and her saint. Julian called during grace. Wes was in the kitchen. ‘Go back to your family, Youngstown.’ Handed Julian the bell rope at Sully’s. Knows I don’t work Mondays. Texted at two in the morning about Yusuf’s mother. On the lawn at four, looking at the place I wasn’t. Came to the Anchor at the end of my shift in Kevin’s car — Julian’s in Oakland, his brother’s home from the Navy. She has a paper. St. Nicholas Eve: Walgreens at half past one. I told her about Ma’s two hundred shoes; she said then we’re doing it, and we did every door in Delgado. Says I hold my phone like a hand of cards. Asked where I go. I said sometime. She said okay. Book Nine, for her Greek final: *Outis*. Nobody. In the laundry room she stepped back first. ‘Don’t make me be the one who wrecks something.’ Julian’s writing something she can’t hear yet. Twelve and oh in overtime. Her free hand found Kevin. Knows Book Nine by heart; asked me to pray at eight. Picked my best argument at the Brick: what a man says yes to. Put her phone face up next to mine and said nothing. Heard Julian’s song before anybody. ‘It’s good, Jack. It’s really good.’ Told me not to leave in the second chorus. The Advent party: I kept the whole room between us all night. She brought coffee to the white elephant, and I got it. Stole my 8-Ball. Won an argument about ‘Joy to the World’ with Isaac Watts. Didn’t play. Julian did. Friday night, half past twelve, she knocked on 412; Theo said the library. At the Mañanitas she told me about Juan Diego, who took the long way around the hill. Thirteen and oh. She texted me the number. After the Gaudete Mass she asked the 8-Ball something. Better not tell you now. Geminids from the roof without me. At Hale’s oral she’d answered him in Augustine — said my sentence was his. She defended it and won, and told him to ask where I say yes at two in the morning. Julian kissed her goodbye at his car; he’s going to New Orleans for New Year’s. Friday she knocked with two coffees and a list of every place. She played the basement piano for me, properly. Taught me a secret in the O Antiphons. Pecan at Gloria’s counter; fourteen and oh is ordained. On the Lighthouse porch she said it plain: I’d never not answered her before. Never missed Sully’s. Always came to her, whatever it was — and now I stay away. She knows something’s hurting. She didn’t make me say what. Walked past the last house to the Point for the first time all semester. The bonfires on the levee on Christmas Eve — call her from the garage. On the roof I nearly said it. The 8-Ball said ask again later. She gave me the tin to keep. I gave her Benedict. At the checkpoint she turned around and said something I couldn’t hear. Christmas week: her sister had the baby in the third quarter of the Dallas game, while they were still undefeated, so Beau didn’t get a vote. Lucille Odile — both grandmothers. Lena’s the godmother. Then they lost. The 8-Ball said very doubtful. She texts me the O Antiphons at dusk. Monday night she called at ten to one to argue about Pius, and won the point fair. I told her I’ve been sleeping in Danny’s bed. She said somebody ought to. When the Pope went down she texted within the minute: is he alright, are you. Christmas Eve she held the phone up to a bonfire on the levee so I could hear it burn. After Midnight Mass she wrote from the steps of Holy Rosary: an hour behind me, like she said. She’d mailed me *The Moviegoer* before the last night. Christmas night she told me how Réveillon went, and about the place her mother sets for her grandmother. Then she said her mama worked at Memorial. Nothing else. Holy Family: they lost to Tampa in overtime — ‘They’re resting.’ Fr. Dom took the short form; hers read the long one, and we’re not discussing it. Sunday night we whispered for two hours because Nonna was asleep in her chair, and she whispered too, from her back steps. I read her her own margins; she argued with the girl who wrote them. I told her Dad went in. ‘And Danny drank it.’ Julian calls at ten his time. Tuesday she called from behind the register at her father’s market — home field; her father’s making the musician a gumbo. I told her what Danny asked about the third. If Pop won’t get out of the truck, she says, I get in. She said she wouldn’t call as much. Then she said she’d call. Wednesday nothing. Thursday at dawn, the morning after Julian landed, she called from the river with beignets. She said she’d call. She asked if I asked Ma who the candle was for. No. You don’t. New Year’s Eve she texted at my midnight, an hour early for her. At hers it came the second the year turned — before the fireworks. I know what that means. Then the river on fire, and Julian beside it. New Year’s Day I called her from the garage at the half, and she said, You called *me*. Saturday night she called the house — Ma answered and talked to her for ten minutes. Two hours on the kitchen phone, her mother’s cordless dying twice. Her grandmother made the christening gown for Luc in 1985; it rode out the storm in Mémère’s cedar chest in Breaux Bridge. She had me be the priest so she could practice the promises. She thinks Binx doesn’t stop looking — he stops looking by himself. I told her Danny asked me something I can’t answer yet; she didn’t ask what. She asked how California was. ‘Come back, Youngstown.’ Two hours, and she never said Julian’s name. Lucille was baptized in the third quarter, and she didn’t get one word wrong. After that I called every night. Twelfth Night she got the baby in the king cake. Friday she said she hasn’t been fair to Julian, and she’s going to fix it. Sunday she landed: come find me tomorrow. Monday I couldn’t find her — not at 217, not at the twelve-ten. She came into Hale’s seminar a step behind him with a king cake, and the only chair left was next to mine. She was polite to me for fifteen minutes. Then Dido. Tuesday morning Julian put up a picture from their dinner Monday — birthday dinner, two days late. She’s tagged. She’d said call me after. I didn’t. At the mailboxes she asked about my break, and I told her as far as Denver, and Ma’s words about the coffee. ‘Tell her I’m glad.’ The baptism was lovely. Tuesday night at St. Brendan’s she had the whole thing organized by half past eight, in a whisper, and put me on the table with Becca. When the TV said trapped she left the room. Julian went. Wednesday at the table she met Skye. She said no pictures at the table, and I argued with her about it in front of everybody. That night at the desk: Skye’s envelope was the biggest. ‘Tell her thank you. From Newman.’ Thursday she took the far end of Hale’s table before anybody got there. She moved the Saints to Sully’s. Saturday in the back hall she said she changed her mind, and stood up for Laney, and said Skye gave a good performance, and wouldn’t say what she meant. At Atlanta she kept my chair till the half. At ten after three she told me the time. Wednesday at three in the morning, the aftershock, in the Fishbowl: she said I could stop whatever I’m doing. I don’t know what I’m doing. Thursday Hale read her whole name off his list. She told him Lena. Saturday she ran the van to San Francisco. Six hours, row three. She asked me if I was happy. I said yes. At the end of the Walk I asked her how she had the nerve to be mad at me. She didn’t answer. She thanked me for coming and left. Monday, when Caleb said I was on a blog, she turned a page. Hale gave her Sarah Miles to prosecute and me Sarah to defend. Wednesday at his house, with the President on, she didn’t drink her wine. A website on Monday, a bed on Tuesday, an iPad before lunch — she had the whole week. She said she had to find out about my girlfriend from a Facebook status, when we talked every single day for weeks. I told her that’s what I meant in San Francisco: she as good as told me to. She says she said no such thing — that I’m lying to win an argument about a book. I was on the other end of that phone. I said it was the night for calling people liars, and got the date wrong, and she had the date. Then we said things we’ve never said. I told her she can’t forgive a status. She asked me if I still go up. Hale stood up and stopped it; the dog felt it through the floor. On her way out she told Hale Sarah let him believe he’d been replaced. She walked home up Del Playa with Laney. Friday in the lounge Laney found the taco picture. Lena laughed. Then she saw me. Then she read the rest of the screen and shut the laptop. Monday at the seminar she sat at the far end, and Hale kept her after with the door shut. Candlemas she carried a candle in the procession. Wednesday morning in the lobby she had a legal pad and a trip — New Orleans, Kevin’s mother’s van, her mother’s house — and she said to Theo, not to me, that her daddy says bring the Ohio boy. She was only telling him what he said. It’s not my trip. Thursday night we packed Kevin’s mother’s van without a word to each other. Everything went through Kevin and Laney. We both asked for the way-back; she got it. She wrote WHO DAT · 3 DAYS on the back glass. Friday at five Skye told her to win her game. Safe flight, she said. She rode to the Rincon with her hood up.
